title: Psalms Chapter 137 Quiz - Multi-Level
description: An enhanced quiz on Psalms chapter 137 with Easy, Medium, Hard, and Theological levels. Each level has 15 carefully crafted questions. Choose your difficulty and dive in!

easy.title: Psalms Chapter 137 Quiz - Easy Level
easy.description: Perfect for beginners! Test your basic knowledge of Psalms Chapter 137.

questions.question: Where did the people sit down and weep according to Psalms 137?
questions.correctAnswer: By the rivers of Babylon
questions.explanation: The verse states that they sat down by the rivers of Babylon and wept as they remembered Zion (Psalms 137:1).

questions.question: What did the people hang upon the willows?
questions.correctAnswer: Their harps
questions.explanation: The verse clearly says they hanged their harps upon the willows in the midst thereof (Psalms 137:2).

questions.question: Who required the captives to sing a song?
options: They that carried us away captive
questions.correctAnswer: They that carried us away captive
questions.explanation: Verse 3 says those who carried them away captive required a song from them (Psalms 137:3).

questions.question: What did the captors want the captives to sing?
options: One of the songs of Zion
questions.correctAnswer: One of the songs of Zion
questions.explanation: The captors demanded they sing one of the songs of Zion (Psalms 137:3).

questions.question: True or False: According to Psalms 137, the captives were happy to sing songs of Zion in Babylon.
questions.correctAnswer: False
questions.explanation: The captives questioned how they could sing the LORD's song in a strange land, implying they were not happy to sing (Psalms 137:4).

questions.question: What will happen if the psalmist forgets Jerusalem?
options: Let my right hand forget her cunning
questions.correctAnswer: Let my right hand forget her cunning
questions.explanation: The psalmist says that if he forgets Jerusalem, his right hand will forget its skill (Psalms 137:5).

questions.question: True or False: The psalmist says that if he does not remember Jerusalem, his tongue will cleave to the roof of his mouth.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Verse 6 states that if he does not remember Jerusalem, his tongue will stick to the roof of his mouth (Psalms 137:6).

questions.question: Who does the psalmist ask God to remember on the day of Jerusalem?
questions.correctAnswer: The children of Edom
questions.explanation: The psalmist asks the LORD to remember the children of Edom who said 'Rase it, rase it' toward Jerusalem (Psalms 137:7).

questions.question: True or False: The children of Edom said to destroy Jerusalem to the foundation.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Verse 7 reports that the children of Edom said, 'Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof' (Psalms 137:7).

questions.question: How is the daughter of Babylon described in the psalm?
options: As one who is to be destroyed
As the queen of the earth
questions.correctAnswer: As one who is to be destroyed
questions.explanation: Verse 8 calls the daughter of Babylon one who is to be destroyed (Psalms 137:8).

questions.question: Who will be happy according to Psalms 137:8?
options: He that rewardeth Babylon as it served us
He that sang the songs of Zion
He that wept by the rivers of Babylon
questions.correctAnswer: He that rewardeth Babylon as it served us
questions.explanation: The verse says happy shall he be that rewards Babylon as it served them (Psalms 137:8).

questions.question: What cruel action is mentioned in Psalms 137:9?
options: Dashing little ones against the stones
questions.correctAnswer: Dashing little ones against the stones
questions.explanation: Verse 9 states that happy shall he be who takes and dashes Babylon's little ones against the stones (Psalms 137:9).

questions.question: In Psalms 137, which event comes first?
options: Sitting by the rivers of Babylon and weeping
Being asked to sing songs of Zion
questions.correctAnswer: Sitting by the rivers of Babylon and weeping
questions.explanation: The psalm begins with sitting by the rivers of Babylon and weeping before mentioning hanging harps, captors' requests, or Edom's remembrance (Psalms 137:1).

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 137:2 mentions that the harps were hung on fig trees.
questions.correctAnswer: False
questions.explanation: The verse clearly states that the harps were hung upon the willows, not fig trees (Psalms 137:2).

questions.question: What did the captors require besides a song from the captives?
questions.correctAnswer: Mirth
questions.explanation: Verse 3 says they required mirth besides a song, saying 'Sing us one of the songs of Zion' (Psalms 137:3).

medium.title: Psalms Chapter 137 Quiz - Medium Level
medium.description: Ready for more? Apply biblical truths from Psalms Chapter 137 to real-life situations.

questions.question: According to Psalms 137:4, why is it difficult for the captives to sing the LORD's song?
options: Because they have lost their harps
Because they are in a strange land
Because they have forgotten the words
Because the LORD has forsaken them
questions.correctAnswer: Because they are in a strange land
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:4 explicitly states the difficulty in singing the LORD's song is due to being in a strange land, highlighting the challenge of worship during exile.

questions.question: What consequence does Psalms 137:5 state will happen if the speaker forgets Jerusalem?
options: Their right hand will forget its cunning
They will be taken captive again
questions.correctAnswer: Their right hand will forget its cunning
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:5 clearly says that if the speaker forgets Jerusalem, their right hand will forget its skill or cunning, symbolizing loss of ability or usefulness.

questions.question: How does Psalms 137:6 describe the speaker's commitment to remembering Jerusalem?
options: Their tongue will cleave to the roof of their mouth
They will dance before the LORD
They will build a new temple
questions.correctAnswer: Their tongue will cleave to the roof of their mouth
questions.explanation: In Psalms 137:6, the speaker expresses that if they do not remember Jerusalem or prefer it above their chief joy, their tongue will stick to the roof of their mouth, symbolizing an inability to speak.

questions.question: What does Psalms 137:5-6 teach about the priority of Jerusalem in the speaker's life?
options: Jerusalem should be remembered only occasionally
Jerusalem is to be remembered above all personal joy and skill
Jerusalem is less important than the harps they hung
Jerusalem is a place to be forgotten for peace
questions.correctAnswer: Jerusalem is to be remembered above all personal joy and skill
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:5-6 emphasize the importance of Jerusalem by stating that forgetting it would cause loss of skill (right hand) and speech (tongue) and that Jerusalem must be preferred above chief joy, showing its supreme priority.

questions.question: What does Psalms 137:6 imply will happen if the speaker does not prefer Jerusalem above their chief joy?
options: Their tongue will cleave to the roof of their mouth
They will wander in the wilderness
questions.correctAnswer: Their tongue will cleave to the roof of their mouth
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:6 clearly states that failure to prefer Jerusalem above chief joy results in the tongue sticking to the roof of the mouth, symbolizing an inability to speak properly.

questions.question: In practical Christian living, what virtue can be drawn from the speaker's vow in Psalms 137:5-6 about remembering Jerusalem?
options: Faithfulness and unwavering commitment to spiritual heritage
questions.correctAnswer: Faithfulness and unwavering commitment to spiritual heritage
questions.explanation: The speaker's vow to never forget Jerusalem and to prefer it above chief joy demonstrates faithfulness and dedication to one's spiritual roots, a key virtue in Christian living (Psalms 137:5-6).

questions.question: How does the question in Psalms 137:4 relate to the emotional state described in Psalms 137:1-3?
options: It expresses the difficulty of worship in exile
It denies the pain of exile
questions.correctAnswer: It expresses the difficulty of worship in exile
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:4's question about singing the LORD's song in a strange land connects to the sorrow and captivity described in verses 1-3, emphasizing the struggle to worship amid suffering.

questions.question: What biblical principle about faithfulness can a believer learn from the vow in Psalms 137:5-6 when facing challenges?
options: Faithfulness requires remembering God and His promises even in hardship
questions.correctAnswer: Faithfulness requires remembering God and His promises even in hardship
questions.explanation: The vow to never forget Jerusalem despite exile (Psalms 137:5-6) illustrates that true faithfulness includes steadfast remembrance of God and spiritual heritage through trials.

questions.question: A fellow believer struggles with discouragement in a foreign environment. Based on Psalms 137:4-6, what biblical truth could encourage them?
options: Worshiping God is impossible outside of your homeland
Remembering and preferring God’s promises above circumstances sustains faith
Giving up on faith is acceptable in exile
One must physically return to Jerusalem to be faithful
questions.correctAnswer: Remembering and preferring God’s promises above circumstances sustains faith
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:4-6 teaches that though singing God's song in a strange land is difficult, remembering Jerusalem and placing it above joy sustains faith even in foreign or challenging situations.

questions.question: True or False: According to Psalms 137:6, if the speaker forgets Jerusalem, their tongue will be unable to speak.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:6 states that if the speaker does not remember Jerusalem or prefer it above chief joy, their tongue will cleave to the roof of their mouth, symbolizing an inability to speak.

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 137:5 promises that forgetting Jerusalem will result in physical blindness.
questions.correctAnswer: False
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:5 says forgetting Jerusalem causes the right hand to forget its cunning, not blindness, emphasizing loss of skill rather than sight.

questions.question: What does Psalms 137:4 teach about worship in difficult circumstances?
options: Worship may be challenging but is still significant
Worship should be abandoned if difficult
questions.correctAnswer: Worship may be challenging but is still significant
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:4 acknowledges the difficulty of singing the LORD’s song in a strange land, highlighting that worship amidst trials is challenging but still important.

questions.question: How do Psalms 137:5-6 emphasize the relationship between memory and identity?
options: Memory of Jerusalem is linked to the speaker's abilities and joy
Memory of Jerusalem is irrelevant to identity
Memory is only about historical facts
questions.correctAnswer: Memory of Jerusalem is linked to the speaker's abilities and joy
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:5-6 tie the memory of Jerusalem to the speaker’s skill (right hand) and speech (tongue), and to their chief joy, showing memory’s central role in identity.

questions.question: What practical lesson about prayer can be drawn from Psalms 137:7 in relation to Psalms 137:4-6?
options: Prayer includes asking God to remember past wrongs and injustices
Prayer is only for personal needs
questions.correctAnswer: Prayer includes asking God to remember past wrongs and injustices
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:7 calls on the LORD to remember the children of Edom who wished destruction on Jerusalem, showing that prayer can involve seeking God's justice, which complements the remembrance theme in verses 4-6.

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 137:6 highlights the importance of preferring Jerusalem above one's chief joy as an expression of faithfulness.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:6 explicitly states the speaker's commitment to place Jerusalem above their chief joy, illustrating a profound expression of faithfulness.

hard.title: Psalms Chapter 137 Quiz - Hard Level
hard.description: Challenge yourself with deep analysis and cross-biblical connections from Psalms Chapter 137.

questions.question: Who are the 'children of Edom' mentioned in Psalms 137:7, and what did they say regarding Jerusalem?
options: They were allies who wished to rebuild Jerusalem
They said, 'Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof'
They were neutral observers of Jerusalem's fate
They prayed for the peace of Jerusalem
questions.correctAnswer: They said, 'Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof'
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:7 states that the children of Edom said, 'Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof,' expressing a desire for Jerusalem's complete destruction.

questions.question: What is the significance of the phrase 'O daughter of Babylon' in Psalms 137:8?
options: It is a term of endearment for the city
It is a metaphor for the city of Babylon personified as a woman to be destroyed
It refers to a literal daughter of a Babylonian king
It symbolizes the people of Israel
questions.correctAnswer: It is a metaphor for the city of Babylon personified as a woman to be destroyed
questions.explanation: In Psalms 137:8, 'O daughter of Babylon' personifies Babylon as a woman destined for destruction, highlighting the theme of judgment against Babylon.

questions.question: What does the Psalmist say about the one who rewards Babylon according to Psalms 137:8?
questions.correctAnswer: They shall be happy
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:8 declares that 'happy shall he be, that rewardeth thee as thou hast served us,' indicating joy for anyone who repays Babylon according to its deeds.

questions.question: What cruel act against children is mentioned in Psalms 137:9?
options: They are dashed against the stones
They are exiled to foreign lands
questions.correctAnswer: They are dashed against the stones
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:9 states, 'Happy shall he be, that taketh and dasheth thy little ones against the stones,' reflecting the harsh judgment and lament against Babylon’s cruelty.

questions.question: Which Old Testament passage echoes the lament and call for justice against Edom found in Psalms 137:7?
questions.correctAnswer: Obadiah 1:10-14
questions.explanation: Obadiah 1:10-14 condemns Edom for standing aloof during Jerusalem’s destruction, echoing Psalms 137:7’s call to remember Edom’s hostility towards Jerusalem.

questions.question: What literary device is exemplified by the repetition of 'Rase it, rase it' in Psalms 137:7?
questions.correctAnswer: Repetition for emphasis
questions.explanation: The phrase 'Rase it, rase it' is an example of repetition to emphasize the total destruction desired against Jerusalem, as seen in Psalms 137:7.

questions.question: How does the theme of retributive justice in Psalms 137:8-9 relate to New Testament teachings?
options: It is fully embraced without question in the New Testament
New Testament teaches forgiveness instead, as in Matthew 5:44
The New Testament repeats the exact same imprecations
There is no connection between these texts
questions.correctAnswer: New Testament teaches forgiveness instead, as in Matthew 5:44
questions.explanation: While Psalms 137:8-9 calls for retributive justice, the New Testament in Matthew 5:44 teaches loving enemies and forgiveness, highlighting a theological development.

questions.question: What is the Hebrew meaning and significance of the word translated 'dasheth' in Psalms 137:9?
questions.correctAnswer: To crush or smash violently
questions.explanation: The Hebrew word 'dasheth' (דָּשַׁת) means to dash or smash violently, emphasizing the harshness of the punishment mentioned in Psalms 137:9.

questions.question: In Psalms 137:7, the plea to 'Remember, O LORD, the children of Edom' is an example of what biblical theme?
options: A call for divine justice against adversaries
questions.correctAnswer: A call for divine justice against adversaries
questions.explanation: The verse is a direct plea for God to bring justice upon Edom, who rejoiced over Jerusalem's downfall, illustrating the biblical theme of divine justice.

questions.question: Which New Testament book contains a typological fulfillment of the theme of exile and restoration found in Psalms 137?
questions.correctAnswer: Revelation
questions.explanation: Revelation contains imagery of Babylon’s fall and the restoration of God's people, thematically fulfilling the exile and judgment themes of Psalms 137.

questions.question: Psalms 137:7-9 closes with imprecations against Babylon. What cultural context helps explain the harshness of these verses?
options: Babylon was a peaceful trading partner
Babylon was the conqueror who destroyed Jerusalem and exiled its people
Babylon was a mythical city with no real history
Babylon was a distant, unrelated nation
questions.correctAnswer: Babylon was the conqueror who destroyed Jerusalem and exiled its people
questions.explanation: The harsh imprecations reflect the trauma of Babylon’s destruction of Jerusalem and exile of Israel, providing historical context for these verses.

questions.question: What is the meaning and significance of 'dashed thy little ones against the stones' in Psalms 137:9 in the ancient Near Eastern context?
options: A literal expression of revenge common in warfare
questions.correctAnswer: A literal expression of revenge common in warfare
questions.explanation: In the ancient Near East, such violent imagery expressed total destruction and revenge against an enemy, reflecting the emotional intensity of Psalms 137:9.

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 137:8 refers to Babylon as a city to be blessed and preserved.
questions.correctAnswer: False
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:8 describes Babylon as 'to be destroyed,' indicating judgment rather than blessing.

questions.question: True or False: Psalms 137:7 uses a form of parallelism common in Hebrew poetry to emphasize the destruction of Jerusalem.
questions.correctAnswer: True
questions.explanation: The verse uses parallelism in the phrases 'Rase it, rase it, even to the foundation thereof' to emphasize total destruction, a common feature in Hebrew poetry.

questions.question: Which earlier Old Testament event does Psalms 137:5-6 allude to by expressing an oath never to forget Jerusalem?
options: The giving of the Ten Commandments
The destruction of the First Temple
questions.correctAnswer: The destruction of the First Temple
questions.explanation: The verses express a deep commitment to remember Jerusalem, reflecting the trauma of the First Temple's destruction and exile.

theological.title: Psalms Chapter 137 Quiz - Theological Level
theological.description: Deep biblical theology from Psalms Chapter 137 that unites all believers. Explore foundational truths about God, creation, and humanity.

questions.question: What does Psalms 137:1 primarily reveal about the emotional state of the exiled Israelites?
options: They were sorrowful and remembered Zion with weeping
They were indifferent to their captivity
questions.correctAnswer: They were sorrowful and remembered Zion with weeping
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:1 clearly states that the Israelites 'wept, when we remembered Zion,' showing their sorrow and lamentation during exile.

questions.question: According to Psalms 137:2, what symbolic action did the captives take with their musical instruments?
options: They hung their harps upon the willows
questions.correctAnswer: They hung their harps upon the willows
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:2 describes how the captives hung their harps upon the willows, symbolizing their mourning and inability to sing joyful songs in captivity.

questions.question: What theological doctrine is illustrated by the captors demanding a song from the captives as stated in Psalms 137:3?
questions.correctAnswer: Doctrine of human depravity
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:3 shows captors cruelly demanding songs from their captives, illustrating human depravity and the hardness of heart that leads to exploitation and mockery.

questions.question: What theological insight about worship in exile is expressed in Psalms 137:4?
options: Worship is only valid in the temple
Worship transcends location and is always possible
Worship is difficult and painful in a foreign land
questions.correctAnswer: Worship is difficult and painful in a foreign land
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:4 questions 'How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?', indicating the difficulty of genuine worship when removed from the sacred context of Jerusalem.

questions.question: Which divine attribute is reflected in the plea of Psalms 137:5 concerning Jerusalem?
questions.correctAnswer: God's faithfulness
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:5 expresses a solemn vow to remember Jerusalem, implying trust in God's faithfulness to preserve His people and city.

questions.question: What combined doctrinal truth is conveyed by Psalms 137:5 and Psalms 137:6 regarding the remembrance of Jerusalem?
options: The importance of joyful singing in exile
The necessity of loving Jerusalem above all earthly joys
The futility of mourning in captivity
questions.correctAnswer: The necessity of loving Jerusalem above all earthly joys
questions.explanation: Verses 5 and 6 emphasize that forgetting Jerusalem is tantamount to losing vital skills and joy, underscoring the doctrine of persevering love and devotion to God's holy city.

questions.question: What does Psalms 137:7 reveal about God's justice in relation to the enemies of Jerusalem?
options: God ignores the enemies of Jerusalem
God remembers and will judge those who destroy Jerusalem
God blesses the enemies for their actions
questions.correctAnswer: God remembers and will judge those who destroy Jerusalem
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:7 petitions God to remember the children of Edom who called for Jerusalem's destruction, highlighting divine justice against oppressors.

questions.question: Which attribute of God is most evident in Psalms 137:8 where the daughter of Babylon is declared destined for destruction?
questions.correctAnswer: God's wrath
questions.explanation: The pronouncement of destruction in Psalms 137:8 reflects God's attribute of wrath toward those who serve evil against His people.

questions.question: How does Psalms 137:9 convey an aspect of divine justice that challenges modern sensibilities?
options: It reveals the severity of God's justice against enemies
It encourages peace at all costs
It calls for passive endurance of injustice
questions.correctAnswer: It reveals the severity of God's justice against enemies
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:9 speaks of harsh judgment on Babylon's children, illustrating the severity of divine justice in the Old Testament context (cf. Nahum 1:2).

questions.question: What narrative arc connection does Psalms 137:1-4 establish within the larger biblical story of Israel's exile and hope?
options: It marks the final restoration of Israel
It depicts Israel's lament and yearning for return to Zion
It recounts Israel's conquest of Babylon
It celebrates the building of the second temple
questions.correctAnswer: It depicts Israel's lament and yearning for return to Zion
questions.explanation: Verses 1-4 situate Israel in exile, mourning Zion, which fits into the broader biblical theme of exile and anticipation of restoration seen throughout the Old Testament (e.g., Jeremiah 29).

questions.question: How do Psalms 137:5-6 and Psalms 137:7 collectively express the tension between remembrance and divine retribution?
options: They emphasize forgetting Jerusalem to avoid pain
They connect faithful remembrance of Jerusalem with a plea for God's righteous judgment on its enemies
They encourage ignoring enemies to focus on personal peace
questions.correctAnswer: They connect faithful remembrance of Jerusalem with a plea for God's righteous judgment on its enemies
questions.explanation: Verses 5-6 vow remembrance of Jerusalem as paramount, while verse 7 petitions God to remember and judge those who destroyed it, illustrating intertwined themes of loyalty and divine justice.

questions.question: What doctrinal teaching about sanctification and joy is drawn from the vow in Psalms 137:6?
options: Joy in worldly pleasures surpasses spiritual commitments
Preferring Jerusalem above chief joy reflects sanctification by aligning joy with God's purposes
Sanctification requires rejecting all forms of joy
questions.correctAnswer: Preferring Jerusalem above chief joy reflects sanctification by aligning joy with God's purposes
questions.explanation: Psalms 137:6 associates true sanctification with valuing Jerusalem—God's holy city—above all earthly joy, teaching that sanctification involves prioritizing spiritual joy.

questions.question: Sceptics claim that Psalms 137 promotes cruel and immoral retribution. What does Psalms 137:7-9 actually teach about God's justice and human response?
options: It reflects a plea for divine justice in the context of profound suffering and injustice
It denies any call for justice
It promotes revenge as a human duty
questions.correctAnswer: It reflects a plea for divine justice in the context of profound suffering and injustice
questions.explanation: Verses 7-9 express longing for God's righteous judgment against oppressors, not human vengeance, highlighting the biblical principle of divine justice (cf. Romans 12:19).

questions.question: What combined theological insight can be drawn from Psalms 137:2 and Psalms 137:3 about worship under duress?
options: Forced worship lacks sincerity and reflects the captors’ cruelty
Worship is always joyful regardless of circumstance
Musical instruments are forbidden in worship
questions.correctAnswer: Forced worship lacks sincerity and reflects the captors’ cruelty
questions.explanation: Verse 2 shows harps hung up in sorrow, while verse 3 records captors demanding songs, illustrating insincere, coerced worship contrasting genuine praise.

questions.question: Which attribute of God is implicitly emphasized by the psalmist's vow in Psalms 137:5 to never forget Jerusalem?
questions.correctAnswer: God's covenant faithfulness
questions.explanation: The vow in Psalms 137:5 reflects confidence in God's covenant faithfulness to Jerusalem and His people, motivating the psalmist's commitment to remember the city.
